slides.title: The Foundation
slides.subtitle: Understanding Stoicism's Origins and Core Principles

mainSections.heading: A Practical Philosophy
text: Stoicism is not abstract theory—it's a living practice. Founded by Zeno of Citium in 301 BCE, it teaches that the path to happiness (eudaimonia) lies in virtue, self-control, and living in harmony with nature and reason.
Unlike philosophies that focus on complex metaphysics, Stoicism offers concrete tools for daily resilience, emotional regulation, and ethical living.

mainSections.heading: The Core Insight
text: Stoicism distinguishes between what we control and what we don't. Our thoughts, judgments, and actions are ours to direct. External events—other people's opinions, the weather, outcomes—are not.
This simple but profound distinction liberates us from anxiety about the uncontrollable and focuses our energy where it matters most: on our own virtue and choices.

quote.text: You have power over your mind—not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength.
quote.author: Marcus Aurelius

slides.title: The Stoic Timeline
slides.subtitle: From Zeno to Marcus Aurelius: Six Centuries of Philosophical Evolution

timeline.name: Zeno of Citium
timeline.description: Taught in the Stoa Poikile (painted porch) in Athens. Established the core doctrine that virtue is the only true good and that we should live in harmony with nature.
timeline.keyInsight: Happiness comes from virtue, not external goods like wealth or reputation.

timeline.name: Cleanthes & Chrysippus
timeline.description: The second and third heads of the Stoic school. Cleanthes emphasized assenting to reason. Chrysippus developed Stoic logic, ethics, and physics, expanding the doctrine into a comprehensive system.
timeline.keyInsight: If Chrysippus had not existed, neither would the Stoa.

timeline.name: Seneca the Younger
timeline.description: Roman statesman and dramatist who wrote accessible essays and letters about applying Stoicism to daily life. Emphasized the shortness of life and the importance of philosophy.
timeline.keyInsight: It is not that we have a short time to live, but that we waste a lot of it.

timeline.name: Epictetus
timeline.description: Born a slave, became one of Rome's greatest philosophers. Taught that true freedom comes from within, emphasizing the dichotomy of control and self-mastery.
timeline.keyInsight: It's not what happens to you, but how you react to it that matters.

timeline.name: Marcus Aurelius
timeline.description: Roman Emperor from 161-180 CE. His private journal, Meditations, reveals a man struggling to maintain virtue under immense pressure. The most powerful man in the world, practicing humility and duty.
timeline.keyInsight: The impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way.

slides.title: The Four Cardinal Virtues
slides.subtitle: The Pillars of Stoic Ethics and the Foundation of the Good Life

virtues.name: Wisdom
virtues.subtitle: Seeing Reality Clearly
virtues.description: The ability to make sound decisions by understanding what's truly good, bad, and indifferent. Wisdom means seeing reality as it is, not as our biases distort it. It's about focusing on what we control and accepting what we don't.
virtues.practice: What's in my control here? Pause before reacting. Examine facts before judgments.

virtues.name: Courage
virtues.subtitle: Acting Rightly Despite Fear
virtues.description: Not just physical bravery, but moral courage—the strength to act according to your principles even when it's difficult, unpopular, or dangerous. Courage means standing firm in life's uncertainties without compromising virtue.
virtues.practice: Speak up for what's right. Face fears incrementally. View challenges as growth opportunities.

virtues.name: Justice
virtues.subtitle: Treating Others Fairly
virtues.description: Marcus Aurelius called justice "the source of all other virtues." It's about acting fairly and kindly toward others, recognizing our shared humanity. Justice means contributing to the common good, not just pursuing self-interest.
virtues.practice: What injures the hive injures the bee. Treat others as ends, not means. Build community.

virtues.name: Temperance
virtues.subtitle: Self-Control and Moderation
virtues.description: Finding balance and avoiding excess. Temperance means choosing long-term well-being over short-term satisfaction. It's the ability to manage desires and emotions rather than being controlled by them.
virtues.practice: Having what is enough. Set boundaries on habits. Resist impulses. Seek simplicity.

content.unityNote: The Unity of the Virtues: The Stoics taught that the virtues are interconnected. You cannot fully have one without the others. Acting with justice requires the wisdom to know what's fair, the courage to stand by it, and the temperance to avoid overreacting.

slides.title: The Dichotomy of Control
slides.subtitle: Epictetus' Foundational Teaching: The Source of Freedom and Peace

epictetus.quote: Some things are within our power, while others are not.
epictetus.explanation: This opening line of the Enchiridion contains the entire Stoic program. Most human suffering comes from confusing these two categories.

withinControl.title: Within Our Control
withinControl.summary: Whatever is of our own doing — our character and choices

beyondControl.title: Beyond Our Control

items.description: What others think, what we own

beyondControl.summary: Whatever is not of our own doing — externals

practice.description: Ask: "What challenges might come today?" Sort them into control categories.
When distressed, pause: "Is this within my control?" If not, let it go.
Focus on your response. Ask: "What would virtue look like here?"

modernExample.controllable: I'll focus on being clear, helpful, and well-prepared

slides.title: Key Stoic Teachers
slides.subtitle: Three Roman Stoics Who Shaped the Philosophy

teachers.name: Seneca
teachers.description: Wealthy Roman senator and advisor to Nero. Lived a life of luxury while advocating simplicity. His writings make Stoicism accessible to everyday life.

keyWorks.title: Letters to Lucilius
keyWorks.description: 124 letters offering practical advice on daily challenges

keyWorks.title: Essays
keyWorks.description: "On the Shortness of Life," "On Anger," "On Tranquility of Mind"

coreTeachings: Life is long if you know how to use it
We suffer more in imagination than reality
True wealth is poverty of desires
teachers.quote: Praecogitati mali mollis ictus venit. (If an evil has been pondered beforehand, the blow is gentle when it comes.)

teachers.name: Epictetus
teachers.description: Born a slave, became Rome's greatest philosopher. His teachings focus on freedom through self-mastery and the dichotomy of control.

keyWorks.title: Discourses
keyWorks.description: His teachings as recorded by student Arrian

coreTeachings: Don't explain your philosophy, embody it
teachers.quote: Men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of them.

teachers.name: Marcus Aurelius
teachers.description: The most powerful man in the world, practicing humility. His private journal reveals a man struggling to maintain virtue under immense pressure.

keyWorks.title: Meditations
keyWorks.description: Personal reflections on duty, acceptance, and maintaining virtue while ruling an empire

coreThemes: Accept the things fate binds you to
Be content with what you are
teachers.quote: The happiness of your life depends upon the quality of your thoughts.

slides.title: Premeditatio Malorum
slides.subtitle: Preparing for Adversity Through Negative Visualization

whatItIs.title: What It Is
whatItIs.subtitle: The Stoic practice of rehearsing adversity in advance
whatItIs.description: Literally "the premeditation of evils," this involves anticipating difficulties before they happen—not to dwell in fear, but to prepare the mind. By imagining hardships, we lessen their sting, strengthen our equanimity, and learn to value what we have.

ancientRoots.translation: If an evil has been pondered beforehand, the blow is gentle when it comes.

ancientRoots.example: Each morning, he reminded himself: "The people I deal with today will be meddling, ungrateful, arrogant, dishonest, jealous, and surly." This preparation helped him respond with virtue.

exercises.title: Morning Visualization
exercises.description: Before starting your day, imagine small frustrations you might face—delays, criticism, fatigue. Prepare to meet them with patience.

exercises.title: Contemplate Loss
exercises.description: Choose something you value—health, a friendship, a possession. Imagine losing it. Sit with the discomfort, then feel gratitude that you still have it now.

exercises.title: Rehearse Greater Trials
exercises.description: Take a larger fear—financial loss, illness, death. Ask: "If this came, what would remain within my control?" Picture responding with courage.

content.paradox: By imagining loss, we don't become gloomy—we become grateful. We realize that these outcomes, though harsh, cannot rob us of our ability to act with virtue.
content.clarification: This isn't worst-case spiraling. Premeditatio is brief, structured, and ends in action. It makes you calmer, not gloomier.

slides.title: The Stoic Morning & Evening Routine
slides.subtitle: Daily Practices That Structure Stoic Living

morning.title: Morning Routine
morning.introduction: Marcus Aurelius began each morning by reminding himself of the challenges ahead and preparing to meet them with virtue. This practice takes 10-20 minutes and sets the tone for the entire day.

steps.title: Perspective Taking (5 minutes)
questions: How will I handle them virtuously?
What good things might I take for granted?

steps.title: Stoic Meditation (5-10 minutes)
steps.description: Sit quietly and imagine how you'll respond to setbacks. Visualize difficult people and situations. Prepare yourself so nothing catches you off-guard. End with gratitude for the opportunity to practice virtue.

steps.title: Set Daily Intention
steps.description: Choose one virtue to focus on today. Say: "Today I will practice [wisdom/courage/justice/temperance] in all my actions."

evening.title: Evening Routine
evening.introduction: Seneca wrote: "The mind should be summoned to review its day." This practice creates accountability and ensures continuous learning and improvement.

questions.question: What did I do well today?

steps.title: Review the Day's Events
steps.description: Go through your day chronologically. Examine your responses to challenges. Where did you react emotionally? Where did you act with virtue? Note patterns and areas for growth.

steps.title: Forgive and Plan
steps.description: Forgive yourself for mistakes. Plan how to do better tomorrow. Set one specific intention for improvement.
steps.quote: Don't be discouraged. The mark of progress is not never falling, but rising again more quickly.

content.powerOfHabit: A gem cannot be polished without friction, nor a man perfected without trials. — These daily practices create the structure for lifelong growth in virtue.

slides.title: Stoic Mindfulness
slides.subtitle: Prosoche: Attention to Our Ruling Faculty

definition.title: What is Prosoche?
definition.subtitle: Constant attention to one's ruling faculty and judgments
definition.description: Prosoche (προσοχή) is the Stoic practice of mindfulness—continuously monitoring our thoughts, judgments, and reactions throughout the day. Unlike Buddhist mindfulness which often focuses on bodily sensations, Stoic mindfulness centers on our rational faculty: the seat of judgment and choice.

goal.description: To catch automatic impressions (phantasiai) before they become destructive emotions or actions. To distinguish between:
goal.keyInsight: We can't control what impressions arise, but we can control whether we assent to them. This is where freedom lies.

practice.title: Catch the Impression
practice.description: Notice when a strong emotion arises. Pause and identify the thought that triggered it. Say: "You are just an impression, not the thing itself."

practice.title: Examine the Judgment
practice.description: Ask: "Is this judgment accurate? Is it about something I control? Does it align with virtue?"

practice.title: Choose Your Response
practice.description: Withhold assent if the judgment is false. Redirect your energy toward virtuous action. Focus on what you control.

modernParallel.title: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy
modernParallel.conclusion: Both teach us to examine and challenge our thoughts rather than being controlled by them.

slides.title: Journaling and Self-Reflection
slides.subtitle: The Stoic Practice of Philosophical Writing

tradition.title: The Stoic Tradition of Journaling
tradition.subtitle: Marcus Aurelius' Meditations was a private journal
tradition.description: Never intended for publication, it reveals a man struggling with the same challenges we face today: distraction, anger, discouragement, and the difficulty of maintaining virtue under pressure. His journal was his tool for self-examination and philosophical practice.

whyJournal.description: Monitor your growth in virtue over time
Transform reactive feelings into reasoned responses

content.senecaPractice: What really ruins our character is the fact that none of us looks back over his life. He wrote regular letters as a form of self-reflection.

questions: Where did I act with virtue today?
Where did I fall to passion or fear?
Were they accurate? In my control?
How did my judgments affect my emotions?
What am I grateful for today?
How can I be better tomorrow?

quotes: The people I deal with today will be... meddling, ungrateful, arrogant, dishonest, jealous, and surly.
But I have seen the beauty of good, and the ugliness of evil, and have recognized that the wrongdoer has a nature related to my own.
marcusExample.note: He uses his journal to remind himself of his principles and prepare for challenges.

slides.title: The Philosophical Roots of CBT
slides.subtitle: How Stoicism Became the Foundation of Modern Psychotherapy

directLineage.title: The Direct Lineage
directLineage.subtitle: CBT founders explicitly credited Epictetus as their philosophical precursor
directLineage.description: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy didn't emerge from thin air—it was built on Stoic insights. Aaron Beck and Albert Ellis, the pioneers of CBT, openly acknowledged that the core principle of their therapeutic approach came directly from ancient Stoic philosophy.

epictetus.quote: Men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of them.

cbt.principle: Events don't cause emotional disturbances—our thoughts and beliefs about events do. Change your thinking, change your emotional response.

sharedInsight.beckQuote: The philosophical origins of cognitive therapy can be traced back to the Stoic philosophers... Epictetus wrote in The Enchiridion: 'Men are disturbed not by things but by the views which they take of them.'

pioneers.name: Albert Ellis
pioneers.role: Founder of Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy (REBT)
pioneers.quote: Much of the theory of REBT was derived from philosophy rather than psychology.
pioneers.claim: Ellis said he "rescued Epictetus from near-obscurity and made him famous all over again."

pioneers.name: Aaron Beck
pioneers.quote: The philosophical underpinnings go back thousands of years, certainly to the time of the Stoics, who considered man's conceptions (or misconceptions) of events rather than the events themselves as the key to his emotional upsets.

slides.title: Research Evidence
slides.subtitle: Scientific Studies on Stoicism and Mental Health

sabs.title: The Stoic Attitudes and Behaviors Scale (SABS)
sabs.description: Modern researchers have developed validated scales to measure Stoic beliefs and practices. Studies with thousands of participants worldwide show clear patterns: people who score highly on Stoicism report greater life satisfaction, stronger resilience, and lower levels of anger and anxiety.
sabs.clarification: Conversely, those who practice "stiff-upper-lip stoicism" (emotional suppression) actually do worse—confirming that authentic Stoicism is about wisdom and acceptance, not suppression.

stoicWeek.title: Stoic Week: Measurable Benefits in 7 Days
stoicWeek.description: Annual event where participants live like Stoics for one week. Results show:
stoicWeek.clinicalQuote: When people put Stoicism into practice in their lives, their relationships, stress levels and general well-being all tend to improve. — Dr. Donald Robertson, cognitive-behavioral psychotherapist

mentalHealthBenefits.description: Research shows adopting Stoic perspectives is associated with notable reduction in anxiety and depression symptoms.
Stoic principles significantly enhance emotional resilience and capacity to cope with life's difficulties.
Stoicism provides a buffer against social comparison by emphasizing internal standards over external validation.
Stoic principles significantly reduce perceived stress and promote psychological well-being.

content.sabsAsTool: The Stoic Attitudes and Behaviors Scale works like both a mirror and a map—showing where you're strong and where you might want to grow.

slides.title: Digital Stoicism
slides.subtitle: Ancient Wisdom for the Modern World

modernChallenge.title: The Modern Challenge
modernChallenge.subtitle: Stoicism offers tools for digital wellness
modernChallenge.description: Social media, smartphones, and information overload create new challenges: constant distraction, comparison culture, and the need for external validation. Stoic principles provide a framework for maintaining autonomy and peace of mind.

dichotomyOnline.title: The Dichotomy of Control Online
dichotomyOnline.keyInsight: Stoicism doesn't reject technology—it guides us to use it virtuously, with clear intentions and boundaries.

strategies.title: Intentional Posting
strategies.description: Ask: "Am I adding value or seeking validation?" Post to be helpful, not to feed ego.

strategies.title: Digital Temperance
strategies.description: Set clear boundaries: time limits, no-phone zones. Practice moderation in all digital consumption.

strategies.title: Negative Visualization
strategies.description: Counter the highlight-reel effect by remembering: social media shows curated moments, not full reality.

strategies.title: Mindful Consumption
strategies.description: Curate your feed intentionally. Unfollow accounts that trigger comparison or unhealthy emotions.

mindfulScroll.title: The Mindful Scroll
questions: Why am I opening this app?
What would virtue look like here?
Am I in control, or is the algorithm?

realWorldScenarios.stoicResponse: I can't control their opinion. I can control my effort and integrity. Let me focus on doing good work and responding with reason, not defensiveness.
This person is not my enemy but a fellow human being. What would justice look like here? Let me listen to understand, not to win.
Wealth is indifferent. True wealth is virtue and contentment. I will focus on what I control: spending wisely, saving consistently, and not worrying about external events.
This is not a tragedy but an opportunity to practice virtue. What can I learn? How can I respond with courage and wisdom? The obstacle becomes the way.

corePrinciples.title: Focus on Virtue
corePrinciples.description: In every situation, ask: "What would wisdom, courage, justice, or temperance look like here?" Let virtue guide your actions.

corePrinciples.title: Accept What Is
corePrinciples.description: Don't demand that events conform to your wishes. Wish that they happen as they do, and your life will flow well.

corePrinciples.title: Practice Daily
corePrinciples.description: Stoicism is a muscle that strengthens with use. Morning reflection, evening review, journaling—these aren't optional extras but essential practice.

corePrinciples.title: Serve the Common Good
corePrinciples.description: We're all part of the same human community. Act for others' benefit, not just your own. Justice is the source of all virtues.

content.reminder: Stoicism isn't about suppression or detachment. It's about transforming your perspective to live with greater wisdom, courage, justice, and temperance—finding strength in virtue rather than externals.

messages: You have power over your mind—not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength.
The path to the good life begins not with changing the world, but with mastering yourself.
Start today: practice virtue, focus on what you control, and meet adversity with wisdom.

quote.text: The impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way.
